title: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Chemical Plants | Dye PT (US)
description: Dye penetrant inspection of stainless, duplex, nickel alloy and aluminum equipment in US chemical plants, with low-sulfur, low-halogen materials. Get a quote.
h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Stainless and Alloy Chemical Processing Equipment (US)
html:
Dye penetrant inspection is the surface-crack method for the stainless steel, duplex, nickel alloy, aluminum and titanium equipment that fills the corrosive end of a chemical plant. Atlantis NDT mobilizes technicians across the United States to examine welds, nozzles, tubesheets, castings and weld repairs on process vessels, piping, heat exchangers and reactors, using low-contaminant penetrant systems chosen for your alloy. To scope an examination, request a PT inspection quote.

Why penetrant is the main surface method in chemical processing

Chemical plants pick alloys to survive the fluid: 304 and 316 stainless for many acids and solvents, duplex grades where chloride is present and strength matters, nickel alloys for hot acids and halogens, aluminum for some oxidizing services and titanium for chlorine and wet bromine. None of these can be examined with magnetic particles, because they are not ferromagnetic, and that makes liquid penetrant testing the working tool for surface cracking. It also covers carbon steel when a coating or rough profile defeats particles, and it shows cracks in welds, castings, forgings and machined parts at their true length.

The same alloys that suit the process are prone to specific forms of cracking. Chloride stress corrosion cracking attacks austenitic stainless steel where tensile stress, chloride and temperature combine, including under insulation and at the outside of vessels exposed to wet chloride-bearing atmospheres, and it appears as fine branching surface cracks. Polythionic acid cracking affects sensitized stainless steel and nickel alloys during shutdowns when sulfur compounds meet moisture and air. Fatigue cracks at nozzle fillets, thermal fatigue at quench and mixing points, and weld solidification cracks in alloy welds all open to the surface. All of them are penetrant targets.

Regulatory and code basis

US chemical plants covered by OSHA's Process Safety Management standard, 29 CFR 1910.119, must keep a mechanical integrity program for process equipment, and EPA's Risk Management Program, 40 CFR Part 68, adds related obligations for listed substances. These regulations require inspection and testing to recognized good engineering practice without naming penetrant. The codes that do are ASME Section VIII for vessels, ASME B31.3 for process piping and the National Board Inspection Code for repair and alteration, along with owner specifications for alloy equipment.

Technique comes from ASTM E165 and ASTM E1417 and, where a code or contract cites it, ASME Section V Article 6, which our Article 6 guide describes in plain terms. Acceptance criteria are set by the code or specification the contract names, and the plant's inspector or authorized inspector applies them. Our technicians work under Atlantis's written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A; a Level II performs the test and evaluates the results, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews each report before release.

The contaminant question on stainless and nickel alloys

This is the part of chemical plant PT that most generic procedures skip. Penetrant materials contain sulfur and halogens, and on austenitic stainless steel, nickel-base alloys and titanium these elements can cause damage when they remain on the metal and the part later sees heat or process fluids. Article 6 limits the sulfur and halogen content of materials used on those alloys, and we supply certificates for the penetrant, remover and developer lot numbers so your quality group has them on file. Where an owner's specification is stricter, the stricter limit is written into the procedure.

After testing, the surface is cleaned to remove penetrant residue, remover and developer, because residues can concentrate under heat or cause trouble in a later weld. For equipment going back into oxygen or other cleaned service, the owner's cleaning specification governs and we coordinate the final clean with the plant. We do not use wire brushes that have touched carbon steel on stainless; dedicated stainless tools prevent cross-contamination and rust staining, and the procedure names that rule.

Equipment and weld types we examine

Welds. Butt welds, fillets, nozzle attachments and weld overlays on process vessels and piping. See the job page on penetrant testing of welds for the full technique. Root and final passes can both be examined where the code requires, and the report states which pass was inspected.

Stainless steel vessels and piping. Examination for stress corrosion cracking, fatigue and fabrication defects. The penetrant testing of stainless steel page covers contamination control and surface condition in detail. Surface finish affects the result: a mechanically polished or electropolished surface can hide fine cracks if the penetrant is removed too aggressively, so the technician adjusts removal.

Heat exchangers and tubesheets. Tube-to-tubesheet welds, channel and shell welds, and tubesheet ligaments are checked on exchangers pulled for repair. Cracks at tube-to-tubesheet joints are a common cause of cross-leakage in corrosive service. Where tube wall condition is the question, specialist tube inspection techniques exist that we do not offer.

Castings. Pump casings, valve bodies, impellers and fittings in stainless and nickel alloys. Porosity and shrinkage cracks show at the surface, and examination of castings uses a developer and dwell suited to rough surfaces; see penetrant testing of castings.

Weld repairs and overlays. Corrosion-resistant weld overlays, clad restoration and repair welds are examined at each stage the specification calls for.

Aluminum and titanium parts. Process equipment in these alloys requires careful cleaning and the correct penetrant chemistry; mechanical cleaning that smears metal is avoided.

Technique details for plant conditions

Cleaning comes first and decides the result. Process residue, scale, polymer, grease and previous dye are removed, using solvents and methods approved for the alloy. Parts that have been in service are often contaminated with product that has to be removed and handled as waste according to site rules. After cleaning, the surface dries completely, because solvent or water left in a crack blocks entry.

Penetrant dwell is set by the procedure and varies with the alloy, the expected defect and the temperature. Cracks that are tight or filled with oxide need longer dwell. Removal is by solvent wipe, water wash or post-emulsification depending on the system, and over-removal is the most common field error, which is why the technician checks a reference panel and uses controlled technique. The developer coat is thin and even, and the part is read in light that suits the penetrant: white light for visible dye, black light and low ambient light for fluorescent.

The standard temperature range in Article 6 is roughly 40 °F to 125 °F. Chemical plant surfaces are often outside it: steam-traced lines, hot vessels and cold-service equipment. In those cases a technician applies a qualified technique, tests it on a comparator block at the working temperature or cools or warms the part. Fluorescent penetrant gives the highest sensitivity for fine stress corrosion cracks, and visible dye is common for outdoor work on larger welds; the report states which.

Where cracks are found, we mark the extent, photograph the indication and tell the plant inspector the same shift. A repair should not start until the engineer has the data, and our job is to hand it over clearly.

Method choice for chemical equipment

Which method for which chemical plant question
QuestionPenetrantOther method
Surface cracks in stainless or nickel alloy weldsPrimary methodMagnetic particle cannot be used
Cracks in carbon steel weldsAlternative on coated or rough surfacesMagnetic particle is usually faster
Wall thinningNot applicableUltrasonic thickness testing
Sub-surface weld flawsCannot see themUltrasonic examination on carbon steel
Porosity in a casting surfaceGoodUltrasonic for internal voids

See the sibling pages ultrasonic testing for chemical processing and magnetic particle testing for chemical processing, and our general comparison of penetrant and magnetic particle methods. For the method across other sectors, start at the national penetrant testing page.

What the PT report contains

  • Equipment tag, weld or part ID, alloy and location within the plant.
  • Procedure number, revision, governing standard and acceptance table applied.
  • Penetrant system, brand and lot numbers, with sulfur and halogen certificates for stainless, nickel and titanium work.
  • Cleaning method, penetrant dwell, removal method, developer and development time.
  • Surface and ambient temperature, and the comparator check if outside the standard range.
  • Lighting conditions and black-light intensity when fluorescent penetrant is used.
  • Examiner and qualification level, with the name of the ASNT Level III who approved the procedure.
  • Each indication with location, size and type, photographed, and an accept or reject call.
  • Post-test cleaning of residue.

What to send for a quote

  1. Equipment list with tags, alloys and the weld or part types to be examined.
  2. The code, specification or repair standard and its acceptance criteria.
  3. Service fluid and temperature, and any cracking history.
  4. Surface finish, coatings, insulation and linings.
  5. Any contaminant limits in your owner specification.
  6. Access, confined space entry rules, site badging and shutdown dates.

Planning realities in a chemical plant

Penetrant waste is hazardous in some sites and ordinary in others, so we ask for the plant's disposal rules before mobilizing. Solvent vapors inside vessels demand ventilation and, in classified areas, equipment and consumables suitable for the classification. Entry to reactors and columns is under the owner's permit, with decontamination and gas testing beforehand. Insulated stainless lines need strips of insulation removed at the points to be examined, usually after a visual check for staining or weeping. Scaffolding and lifts are usually set up by the plant, and we list the points that need access in advance.

We do not perform radiography in the United States, we do not offer specialist tube inspection techniques at this site, and we do not decide whether a vessel is fit for service; those decisions belong to your engineer and inspector.

Training your own penetrant inspectors

Plants that qualify their own technicians can use our SNT-TC-1A-based PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training, with practice in the penetrant testing simulator. The employer certifies its own personnel, so a written practice and a procedure qualification and demonstration are part of the setup, and we can support both.

faq.q: Why is penetrant testing used on stainless steel in chemical plants?
faq.a: Austenitic stainless is not ferromagnetic, so magnetic particle inspection cannot be used. Penetrant finds cracks open to the surface, including chloride stress corrosion cracking and fabrication defects, on welds and parts of any alloy.

faq.q: What penetrant materials do you use on stainless and nickel alloys?
faq.a: Low-sulfur, low-halogen systems that meet the contaminant limits in ASME Section V Article 6 and your own specification. We record lot numbers and keep the certificates so your quality group can file them with the report.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing find chloride stress corrosion cracking?
faq.a: Yes when the cracks are open to the surface. They show as fine, branching lines on cleaned stainless steel. Cracks under insulation need the insulation opened first, and your engineer decides which locations to examine.

faq.q: Does surface finish affect the result on polished stainless?
faq.a: Yes. Polished or electropolished surfaces can hide fine cracks if the penetrant is over-removed. The technician adjusts removal and checks the system on a reference panel before production work.

faq.q: Can PT be done on hot or cold equipment?
faq.a: The standard technique covers roughly 40 °F to 125 °F. Outside that range we demonstrate a qualified technique on a comparator block at the working temperature, or the part is warmed or cooled first.

faq.q: Who decides if a penetrant indication is acceptable?
faq.a: The code table in your contract or specification, applied by your inspector or authorized inspector. We record location, size and type and compare each indication to the named criteria.

faq.q: Do you leave residue in the vessel after testing?
faq.a: No. We clean the area of penetrant, remover and developer afterwards and record the cleaning in the report. Oxygen or other cleaned service follows your cleaning specification, coordinated with the plant.

faq.q: Can you examine heat exchanger tubes with penetrant?
faq.a: We examine tube-to-tubesheet welds, channel and shell welds and tubesheet surfaces accessible from the outside. The internal condition of the tube wall needs specialist techniques that Atlantis does not offer on this page.

faq.q: What do you need to quote chemical plant PT work?
faq.a: An equipment list with alloys, the weld or part types, the code and acceptance table, service fluid and temperature, contaminant limits, surface condition and access, and the site's permit and shutdown details.
